# Question 3: Web Text Mining

## Question 3.1: Web scraping and text extraction

```{r}
# Had to install packages as they weren't installed

for (package in packages) {

    install.packages(package)
  }
}
```

```{r}
# Load the packages
library(rvest)
library(httr)
library(robotstxt)
```

```{r}
# My chosen website is Books to Scrape, a website designed for
# practising web scraping.

website_url <- "https://books.toscrape.com/"

# I selected the book "Join" for the text analysis 
book_url <- paste0(
  website_url,
  "/catalogue/join_902/index.html"
)

# Check whether the website's robots.txt rules allow access

scraping_allowed <- paths_allowed(book_url)

# Display the result of the access check
scraping_allowed
```
Books to Scrape was selected because it is a demonstration website designed for practising web scraping. The robots.txt check returned TRUE, but also reported that the file was not found, so the result was not treated as confirmation of an explicit robots.txt permission. The demonstration requests one selected book page.

```{r}
# Read the selected book page
book_page <- read_html(book_url)

# Extract the book title
book_title <- book_page |>
  html_element("h1") |>
  html_text2()

# Extract the paragraph after the product-description heading
book_description <- book_page |>
  html_element("#product_description + p") |>
  html_text2()

# Store the extracted details in a data frame
book_data <- data.frame(
  title = book_title,
  content = book_description,
  source_url = book_url,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Check the extracted title and description
book_data
```
```{r}
# Check that the description was extracted
cat(book_data$content)
```
## Explanation: 
The extracted book title and description were stored in an R data frame named book_data. The data frame contains one row representing the selected webpage, with columns for the title, extracted content and source URL.


## Question 3.2: Textual data preprocessing
```{r}
# Install tm
if (!requireNamespace("tm", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("tm")
}

library(tm)

```
```{r}
# Keep the original extracted text unchanged
original_text <- book_data$content

# Remove the duplicated opening.
starts <- gregexpr("What if you could live multiple lives",
                   original_text, fixed = TRUE)[[1]]

if (length(starts) >= 2 && starts[2] > 0) {
  cleaned_text <- substring(original_text, starts[2])
} else {
  cleaned_text <- original_text
}

# Add a space where sentence-ending punctuation is followed
# immediately by a capital letter, e.g. "horrors.Jolted"
cleaned_text <- gsub(
  "([.!?])([A-Z])",
  "\\1 \\2",
  cleaned_text,
  perl = TRUE
)

# Remove the website's trailing
cleaned_text <- sub("\\s*\\.\\.\\.more\\s*$", "", cleaned_text)

# Remove extra whitespace
cleaned_text <- trimws(gsub("\\s+", " ", cleaned_text))

# Save the cleaned text alongside the original
book_data$cleaned_content <- cleaned_text

# Inspect the cleaned text
cat(book_data$cleaned_content)
```

```{r}
# Start with the readable cleaned description
analysis_text <- cleaned_text 

# Convert the text to lowercase 
analysis_text <- tolower(analysis_text)

# Replace punctuation and numbers with spaces 
analysis_text <- gsub("[[:punct:][:digit:]]+", " ", analysis_text)

# Split the text into individual words 
words <- unlist(strsplit(analysis_text, "\\s+"))

# Remove empty entries and common English stopwords 
words <- words[
  words != "" &
  !words %in% stopwords("english")
]

# Create a frequency table for the remaining words 
word_frequencies <- sort(table(words), decreasing = TRUE)

# Display the most common words
head(word_frequencies, 15)
```
### Explanation of text preprocessing
The extracted book description was cleaned to prepare it for analysis.
The repeated opening was removed, missing spaces between sentences were
corrected, and the trailing website marker was removed. Extra whitespace
was also removed.

A separate version was converted to lowercase and split into individual
words. Punctuation, numbers, empty entries and common English stopwords
were removed before calculating word frequencies. The readable cleaned
description was retained for sentence-based summarisation.



## Question 3.3: Text summarisation and visualisation
```{r}
# Install stringr 
if (!requireNamespace("stringr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("stringr")
}
library(stringr)
```
```{r}
# Split the readable description into sentences 
sentences <- str_split(
  cleaned_text,
  "(?<=[.!?])\\s+"
)[[1]]

# Remove empty sentences
sentences <- sentences[nzchar(trimws(sentences))]
# Display the number of sentences available
length(sentences)
```
```{r}
# Score each sentence using the frequencies of the meaningful words
sentence_scores <- sapply(sentences, function(sentence) {

  # Apply the same basic cleaning 
  sentence <- tolower(sentence)
  sentence <- gsub("[[:punct:][:digit:]]+", " ", sentence)

  sentence_words <- unlist(strsplit(sentence, "\\s+"))

  # Keep words that appear in the frequency table
  sentence_words <- sentence_words[
    sentence_words %in% names(word_frequencies)
  ]

  if (length(sentence_words) == 0) {
    return(0)
  }

  # Average the word frequencies to reduce preference for long sentences
  mean(as.numeric(word_frequencies[sentence_words]))
})

# Select the three highest-scoring sentences
n_summary <- min(3, length(sentences))

selected_sentences <- order(
  sentence_scores,
  decreasing = TRUE
)[seq_len(n_summary)]

# Restore their original order 
selected_sentences <- sort(selected_sentences)

# Display the frequency-based summary
cat(
  paste(sentences[selected_sentences], collapse = " ")
)
```
```{r}
# Install textrank
if (!requireNamespace("textrank", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("textrank")
}

library(textrank)
```
```{r}
# Create a data frame with an ID for each sentence
sentence_data <- data.frame(
  textrank_id = seq_along(sentences),
  sentence = sentences,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Prepare words for each sentence
sentence_tokens <- lapply(seq_along(sentences), function(i) {

  # Convert to lowercase and remove punctuation and numbers
  text <- tolower(sentences[i])
  text <- gsub("[[:punct:][:digit:]]+", " ", text)

  # Split into words and remove common English stopwords
  tokens <- unlist(strsplit(text, "\\s+"))
  tokens <- tokens[tokens != "" & !tokens %in% tm::stopwords("english")]

  data.frame(
    textrank_id = rep(i, length(tokens)),
    term = tokens,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})

# Combine the words from all sentences into one table
terminology <- do.call(rbind, sentence_tokens)

# Rank sentences using TextRank
textrank_result <- textrank_sentences(
  data = sentence_data,
  terminology = terminology
)

# Show the top three sentences in their original order
textrank_summary <- summary(
  textrank_result,
  n = 3,
  keep.sentence.order = TRUE
)

textrank_summary
```
### Comparison of the summarisation techniques

Both the frequency-based method and TextRank selected the same three
sentences. The frequency-based method ranked sentences according to the
average frequency of their meaningful words, whereas TextRank ranked
sentences according to their connections with other sentences based on
shared words.

The selected sentences describe the Join technology, Chance and Lucky's
search for a cure, and their encounter with the creators of a new form
of consciousness. Because the source description is short, the results
are exploratory. The summary also begins with “That’s the promise”,
which refers to an omitted sentence; this illustrates how extractive
summaries can lose context.


```{r}
# Install ggplot2 if needed
if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("ggplot2")
}

library(ggplot2)

# Convert the 10 most frequent words into a data frame
top_words <- as.data.frame(head(word_frequencies, 10))
colnames(top_words) <- c("word", "frequency")

# Create a labelled bar chart
ggplot(top_words, aes(x = reorder(word, frequency), y = frequency)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#E85D9E") +
  geom_text(aes(label = frequency), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Most frequent words in the book description",
    subtitle = "After text preprocessing and stopword removal",
    x = "Word",
    y = "Frequency (number of occurrences)",
    caption = "Source: Books to Scrape"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
## Findings: Word frequency
The pink bar chart above presents the ten most frequent words in the book description after text preprocessing and stopword removal. The words “technology”, “join” and “human” each appear three times, making them the most frequent words in the cleaned text. The words “consciousness”, “chance” and “lucky” each appear twice.

The results suggest that the description focuses on technology and human consciousness, as well as the experience of the two main characters. The book description is relatively short, so the frequencies are low and should be interpreted in the context of this single text.

```{r}
library(wordcloud)


set.seed(123)

# Reserve space above and below the word cloud
par(mar = c(4, 1, 5, 1))

wordcloud(
  words = names(word_frequencies),
  freq = as.numeric(word_frequencies),
  max.words = 30,
  min.freq = 1,
  random.order = FALSE,
  colors = c("#E754A3", "#A65DD8", "#20A6A1"),
  scale = c(3, 0.7)
)

title(
  main = "Most frequent words in the book description",
  line = 2,
  cex.main = 1.2
)

mtext(
  "Word size represents frequency",
  side = 1,
  line = 2,
  cex = 0.9
)
```
## Findings: Word Cloud 
The above word cloud presents the most frequent words in the cleaned description of Join. Larger words appear more frequently in the text. The words “human”, “technology”, and “join” are among the largest, while “consciousness”, “chance” and “lucky” are also visible.

These words highlight the descriptions focus on technology, human consciousness and experiences of the two main characters. The word cloud complements the bar chart by providing a visual overview of the vocabulary, while the bar chart shows the exact frequencies. Both visualisations are based on the same short book description.
